client:
I just feel so numb all the time lately. Before the accident, Mark and I used to go hiking every weekend - it was our thing. Now when I try to go alone, it just makes me angry that he's not there, so I end up turning around and going home. 

I don't know if talking about this will help. Everything just feels pointless without him, and I don't see how therapy can change that. How am I supposed to enjoy things when the person I enjoyed them with is gone?
therapist:
It sounds like you’re carrying a deep sense of loss and emptiness, especially when you try to reconnect with activities that used to bring you joy with Mark. That anger and frustration when you attempt to go hiking alone—could we explore what thoughts come up in those moments when you decide to turn back?  

I hear how hopeless this feels right now, and I’d gently ask: What do you think Mark would want for you in this grief? Sometimes, the answers we’re searching for come from the love that still connects us.

client: I don't know what Mark would want for me - that's part of why I'm so stuck. When I try to think about that, I just get angry that he's not here to tell me himself. The last time I tried to hike our favorite trail, I kept imagining him laughing at me for being so pathetic, struggling up the path alone. It's easier to just stay home.
therapist:
I hear how painful it is to feel like you’re losing those precious memories—even imagining his laughter now brings anger instead of comfort. It makes sense that staying home feels safer when those thoughts show up.  

When that voice says you’re "pathetic" struggling alone, do you think that’s truly how Mark would see you, or could grief be twisting those thoughts? Let’s slow down and untangle this together.

client:
I don't know how Mark would see me anymore. That's the worst part - I keep trying to remember how he used to comfort me when I was upset, but now those memories just make me feel angrier at myself for falling apart. 

It's not just grief twisting things - it's the fact that I *am* struggling alone, and he's not here. That's the reality, isn't it? No amount of untangling changes that.
therapist:
The pain feels so real because the loss *is* real—no amount of reframing will change that truth, and I’d never want to minimize that. But I wonder if we could gently separate two things: the unchanging fact of his absence, and the judgments you’re layering on top of it.  

When you say you’re “falling apart,” what does that look like to you? Is it possible that what feels like weakness might actually be your strength—your capacity to love him so deeply still showing through, even in grief?

client: I know you're trying to help, but when you say my grief might be strength... it just makes me feel more guilty. Because if this is strength, then why do I feel so broken all the time? I can't eat properly, I cry at random moments, and some days I can't even get out of bed. That doesn't feel like strength to me.
therapist:
I hear how exhausted you are—how the weight of grief makes even basic things feel impossible right now. That doesn’t mean you’re broken; it means you’re human, and your body and mind are carrying a love that has nowhere to go.  

Could we try something different? Instead of judging whether this is "strength" or "weakness," what if we simply noticed what’s happening? When the tears come or the bed feels heavy, what’s the *kindest* interpretation you could offer yourself in those moments?

client:
I don't know if I can be kind to myself right now. Every time I try, it just feels like I'm making excuses for falling apart. The grief is so heavy that even small kindnesses feel like lies—like pretending this pain isn't completely swallowing me whole. 

And when you say "a love that has nowhere to go," that just makes it worse because it's true, and facing that truth hurts more than the numbness did.
therapist:
I hear how raw and unbearable this pain feels—how even the idea of kindness can’t pierce the weight of your loss right now. That’s okay; we don’t have to force anything.  

When the numbness felt safer, what did it protect you from that feels too sharp to face now? Sometimes just naming that fear can take some of its power away.

client:
I think the numbness protected me from feeling like a failure. My dad was sick for so long, and I kept thinking if I just did more—found better doctors, pushed harder—maybe he'd still be here. Now when the grief hits, it's not just sadness, it's this crushing guilt that I didn't do enough. 

But naming it... I don't know if that helps. It just makes it more real, like admitting I failed him.
therapist:
That guilt sounds like it’s carrying so much pain—this belief that you could have or should have done more for your dad. It makes me wonder: if someone you loved were in your shoes, feeling this way about their own loss, would you tell them they’d failed? Or might you see how deeply they cared?  

The grief is real, and so is the love behind it. What would it feel like to let those exist together, even for just a moment, without the weight of "should haves"?

client:
That's... hard to hear. I mean, of course I wouldn't tell someone else they'd failed if they were grieving. But it feels different when it's me. The "should haves" just keep playing in my head - I should've visited more, should've called more. The love is there, but it's buried under so much regret. 

It's like I know logically I did what I could, but my heart won't accept that. The guilt feels like the only thing keeping me connected to him now, if that makes any sense.
therapist:
It makes complete sense—that guilt has become a kind of bridge to your dad, even though it’s a painful one. It’s almost as if letting go of the "should haves" might feel like letting go of *him*, and no wonder that terrifies you.  

What if we tried something small? When those thoughts come—"I should’ve called more"—could you pause and add one gentle sentence: "And I did what I could with what I knew then"? Not to erase the guilt, but to make space for the love beneath it. How does that sit with you?

client:
I get what you're saying, but when I try to add that gentle sentence, it just makes me feel worse. Like I'm making excuses for not being there enough. The guilt feels like the only thing proving how much I cared about him. 

It's not that I don't want to try, but whenever I attempt to be kinder to myself about it, I get this panicky feeling like I'm betraying his memory somehow. Does that make sense?
therapist:
I hear how scary it feels to loosen that grip on guilt—like you’re risking the last thread tying you to your dad. That panic makes so much sense when the guilt has been carrying all your love for him.  

What if we didn’t try to replace the guilt yet, but just noticed how tightly you’re holding it? When that panicky feeling comes, where do you feel it in your body? Sometimes giving it space—not fighting it—softens its edges.

client:
It's weird, but I feel that guilt like a heavy weight right in my chest. When I try to notice it instead of pushing it away, I just start crying. That makes me panic more because it feels like if I stop punishing myself, I'm forgetting him. 

I don't know if noticing it helps - the pain just feels sharper when I pay attention to it. Doesn't that mean the guilt is important? Like it's keeping me connected to him?
therapist:
That weight in your chest—it’s not just guilt, is it? It’s all that love with nowhere to go, and the terrible fear that if the pain eases even a little, you’ll lose him all over again. The crying isn’t weakness; it’s your heart insisting, *He mattered*.  

What if the connection isn’t in the guilt, but in how deeply you *still* care? When you imagine letting that weight shift—not disappear, just change shape—what’s the scariest part? And what’s the tiniest, gentlest possibility?

client:
That idea of the love having nowhere to go... that makes my throat tighten up. I think you're right about the fear too - like if I stop hurting this much, it means I'm forgetting him. But the thought of shifting the weight scares me because what if it just becomes... emptiness? 

The gentlest possibility you mentioned - I can barely let myself imagine that. It feels like betraying him to think there might be another way to carry this.
therapist:
I hear how terrifying that emptiness feels—like you're standing at the edge of losing him all over again if the pain changes. That tightness in your throat? It’s love fighting to stay alive, not just grief.  

What if we didn’t have to choose between agony and emptiness? Could we imagine—even for a breath—that your love for him might find a way to exist *differently*? Not less, just… softer? Where does that idea land in your body right now?
